questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which segment reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered sodium and water?
options: The proximal convoluted tubule, reabsorbing about two-thirds isosmotically
questions.concept: Because reabsorption here is isosmotic, tubular fluid osmolality at the end of the proximal tubule equals plasma, and the concentrating work begins in the loop.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which transporter is inhibited by furosemide, and in which segment?
options: The sodium-potassium-two-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
The sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal tubule
The epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
questions.concept: Blocking it abolishes the medullary gradient so both concentrating and diluting ability are lost, and the increased distal sodium delivery drives potassium and hydrogen loss.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which cell of the collecting duct secretes hydrogen ion and reabsorbs bicarbonate?
options: The alpha-intercalated cell, using an apical hydrogen ATPase
questions.concept: Beta-intercalated cells do the reverse, secreting bicarbonate in alkalosis, and failure of the alpha cell causes distal renal tubular acidosis with an inability to acidify the urine.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which buffer allows the kidney to excrete the largest quantity of acid, and how is its capacity increased in chronic acidosis?
options: Ammonium, whose production from glutamine is upregulated over days
Phosphate, whose filtered load is fixed
questions.concept: Titratable acid excretion is limited by the filtered phosphate load, whereas ammoniagenesis can increase severalfold, which is why the urinary anion gap is used to assess it clinically.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: A patient has arterial pH 7.32, bicarbonate 16 mmol per litre and carbon dioxide tension 32 mmHg. Which disorder is present?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
questions.concept: Winter's formula predicts an expected carbon dioxide of about 32 mmHg for this bicarbonate, so the compensation is appropriate and no second disorder need be invoked.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which finding indicates that a metabolic acidosis has a raised anion gap?
options: Accumulation of an unmeasured anion such as lactate, ketoacid or a toxin metabolite
Loss of bicarbonate with chloride retention
questions.concept: A normal gap acidosis reflects bicarbonate loss with hyperchloraemia, and calculating the delta ratio detects a coexisting metabolic alkalosis or normal-gap acidosis.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Which reflex initiates micturition, and which centre coordinates it?
options: Bladder stretch receptors acting through the pontine micturition centre, with voluntary control from the cortex
A purely spinal reflex with no supraspinal input
Sympathetic outflow from T10 to L2 alone
questions.concept: A suprasacral cord lesion therefore produces a reflex or spastic bladder after the initial areflexic phase, whereas a sacral or conus lesion produces a flaccid atonic bladder.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Why does aldosterone excess cause hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis?
options: It increases sodium reabsorption with potassium and hydrogen secretion in the collecting duct
questions.concept: Volume expansion also raises the filtered load and distal flow, which augments potassium loss, and this explains the biochemical signature of primary hyperaldosteronism.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Why is potassium secretion dependent on distal sodium delivery?
options: Sodium entry through the epithelial sodium channel creates a lumen-negative potential that drives potassium out through apical channels
Potassium is exchanged directly for sodium at the apical membrane
questions.concept: This coupling explains why loop and thiazide diuretics cause hypokalaemia and why potassium-sparing agents that block the channel, or the aldosterone receptor, prevent it.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Renal Tubular Processing and Acid-Base Regulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormone surge triggers ovulation, and what is its source?
options: The luteinising hormone surge from the anterior pituitary, provoked by rising oestradiol
Human chorionic gonadotropin from the ovary
questions.concept: The switch of oestradiol from negative to positive feedback at high sustained concentrations is what generates the surge, and ovulation follows about 36 hours later.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which cell of the testis produces testosterone, and under which trophic hormone?
options: The Leydig cell, under luteinising hormone
The Sertoli cell, under luteinising hormone
The Leydig cell, under follicle-stimulating hormone
questions.concept: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and to secrete inhibin B, which feeds back selectively on follicle-stimulating hormone.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormone maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy until the placenta takes over?
options: Human chorionic gonadotropin from the syncytiotrophoblast
questions.concept: The luteoplacental shift occurs at about 8 to 10 weeks, after which the placenta produces sufficient progesterone and removal of the corpus luteum no longer causes miscarriage.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormonal change immediately after delivery permits the onset of copious milk secretion?
options: The abrupt fall in progesterone while prolactin remains high
questions.concept: Retained placental fragments delay lactogenesis for exactly this reason, and suckling then maintains prolactin secretion by inhibiting hypothalamic dopamine release.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which reflex is responsible for milk ejection, and which hormone mediates it?
options: The neuroendocrine let-down reflex mediated by oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
A local myoepithelial reflex without hormones
questions.concept: Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli, and because the pathway is neural at its afferent limb it is readily inhibited by pain, anxiety and embarrassment.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains lactational amenorrhoea?
options: High prolactin suppresses pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion, preventing ovulation
questions.concept: Because the effect depends on frequent suckling, its contraceptive reliability falls as feeds are spaced or supplemented, which is the physiological basis of the lactational amenorrhoea method's three conditions.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which change in the ovarian cycle is responsible for the rise in basal body temperature in the second half?
options: Progesterone from the corpus luteum acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre
questions.concept: The biphasic temperature chart is therefore evidence that ovulation has occurred, and its absence suggests an anovulatory cycle.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does inhibin allow selective feedback control of follicle-stimulating hormone without affecting luteinising hormone?
options: Inhibin acts specifically at the pituitary gonadotroph to suppress follicle-stimulating hormone synthesis
It converts luteinising hormone to follicle-stimulating hormone
questions.concept: This selectivity underlies the fall in follicle-stimulating hormone that causes atresia of all but the dominant follicle, and its measurement is used as a tumour marker in granulosa cell tumours.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does the fetus not reject the mother, and the mother not reject the fetus, despite their genetic difference?
options: The trophoblast expresses little classical MHC class I and no class II, with local regulatory T cell and cytokine mechanisms creating tolerance
The placenta is an absolute barrier to cells
questions.concept: Fetal cells do cross into the maternal circulation, which is how cell-free fetal DNA testing works and how Rh sensitisation occurs, so the tolerance is active rather than a matter of separation.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Reproductive and Hormonal Functions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which chemoreceptor provides the principal drive to ventilation in response to a rise in arterial carbon dioxide?
options: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla, responding to cerebrospinal fluid hydrogen ion
questions.concept: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier readily while hydrogen ion does not, so central receptors sense pH change in the cerebrospinal fluid and account for most of the carbon dioxide response.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which receptor is responsible for the ventilatory response to a fall in arterial oxygen tension?
options: The carotid body, responding when tension falls below about 60 mmHg
questions.concept: Because the response is flat until tension falls steeply, oxygen provides little drive in health, and this is why the hypoxic drive matters chiefly in chronic carbon dioxide retention.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which reflex terminates inspiration when the lung is greatly inflated?
options: The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex, mediated by vagal slowly adapting stretch receptors
questions.concept: In adults the reflex is largely inactive at normal tidal volumes and becomes important only at high volumes, though it operates during normal breathing in the newborn.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which acid-base change explains why ventilation increases only partially on arrival at high altitude and then rises further over days?
options: Hypoxic drive is initially opposed by hypocapnic alkalosis, which resolves as the kidney excretes bicarbonate
questions.concept: Acetazolamide accelerates this renal bicarbonate loss, which is why it both prevents acute mountain sickness and improves ventilation and sleep at altitude.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does a person hyperventilating before a breath-hold dive risk loss of consciousness under water?
options: Lowering carbon dioxide delays the urge to breathe until oxygen has fallen dangerously low
questions.concept: Because carbon dioxide rather than oxygen drives the urge to surface, removing that stimulus decouples the warning from the danger, producing shallow-water blackout.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which condition causes decompression sickness in a diver ascending too rapidly?
options: Nitrogen dissolved at depth under pressure comes out of solution as bubbles
questions.concept: Controlled ascent with stops allows nitrogen to be eliminated through the lungs, and treatment of established disease is recompression with hyperbaric oxygen.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which pattern of breathing is characterised by cycles of gradually increasing then decreasing tidal volume with intervening apnoea?
options: Cheyne-Stokes respiration, seen in heart failure and at altitude
questions.concept: It arises from an unstable feedback loop with prolonged circulation time and increased chemoreceptor gain, so the ventilatory response overshoots and undershoots repeatedly.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does giving high-concentration oxygen to a patient with chronic carbon dioxide retention risk worsening hypercapnia?
options: It abolishes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening ventilation-perfusion matching, and reduces the hypoxic ventilatory drive
questions.concept: The dominant mechanism is now understood to be the loss of ventilation-perfusion matching rather than drive alone, which is why controlled oxygen to a target saturation of 88 to 92 percent is used rather than withholding oxygen.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why is the ventilatory response to exercise so precise that arterial carbon dioxide barely changes despite a large rise in production?
options: Feed-forward drive from the motor cortex and joint receptors acts with chemoreceptor feedback to match ventilation to metabolism
Carbon dioxide production does not rise
questions.concept: Because arterial carbon dioxide is nearly constant during moderate exercise, chemoreceptor feedback alone cannot explain the response, which is why anticipatory neural mechanisms are invoked.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Regulation of Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Where is cerebrospinal fluid produced and where is it principally absorbed?
options: Produced by the choroid plexus and absorbed through arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses
Produced by the arachnoid and absorbed by the choroid plexus
Produced by ependyma and absorbed by lymphatics only
Produced by the pia and absorbed by capillaries
questions.concept: About 500 mL is produced daily against a total volume of 150 mL, so the fluid turns over three times a day, and obstruction anywhere along the path produces hydrocephalus.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Which receptor cells mediate colour vision, and how many types are there in humans?
options: Cones, of three types with peak sensitivities in the short, medium and long wavelengths
questions.concept: Rods contain a single pigment so they cannot support colour discrimination, which is why colour vision fails in scotopic conditions and why the fovea, which is cone-rich, is used for colour and detail.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Which structure of the inner ear detects angular acceleration, and which detects linear acceleration?
options: The semicircular canals detect angular acceleration and the otolith organs detect linear acceleration and head tilt
questions.concept: Fluid inertia deflects the cupula in the canals, whereas the weight of otoconia on the maculae signals tilt, and displacement of otoconia into a canal causes benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Which stage of sleep is characterised by muscle atonia, rapid eye movements and a desynchronised EEG resembling wakefulness?
options: Rapid eye movement sleep, in which most dreaming occurs
questions.concept: Loss of the normal atonia produces REM sleep behaviour disorder, which may precede Parkinson disease by years, and REM proportion is greatest in the newborn.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Which set of thermoregulatory responses is initiated by the hypothalamus in a cold environment?
options: Cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering, piloerection and increased thyroid and sympathetic activity
questions.concept: The preoptic anterior hypothalamus integrates skin and core temperature, and non-shivering thermogenesis in brown fat is the dominant mechanism in the newborn who cannot shiver.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: How does fever differ physiologically from hyperthermia?
options: In fever the hypothalamic set point is raised by prostaglandin E2 so heat-conserving responses operate, whereas in hyperthermia the set point is normal and the mechanisms are overwhelmed
Fever has no set point change
questions.concept: This is why antipyretics work in fever but not in heat stroke, and why a febrile patient feels cold and shivers while a hyperthermic patient does not.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains presbyopia?
options: Loss of lens elasticity with age reduces the amplitude of accommodation
Weakness of the ciliary muscle alone
questions.concept: Because the lens itself hardens, the near point recedes progressively from childhood and becomes symptomatic in the fifth decade, requiring a convex reading addition.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Why does conductive hearing loss cause the Weber test to lateralise to the affected ear?
options: Removal of masking ambient air-conducted sound makes the bone-conducted signal appear louder on the affected side
The auditory nerve is stimulated directly
questions.concept: In sensorineural loss the cochlea itself is impaired so the sound lateralises to the better ear, and combining Weber with Rinne allows the type of loss to be identified at the bedside.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Special senses, CSF, temperature regulation & sleep
questions.stem: Why does the blood-brain barrier make cerebrospinal fluid analysis useful in diagnosing central nervous system infection?
options: The barrier normally excludes cells, most proteins and immunoglobulin, so their appearance indicates local inflammation or synthesis
Cerebrospinal fluid is identical to plasma
The barrier admits all solutes equally
Antibody is always transferred from blood
questions.concept: Oligoclonal bands present in cerebrospinal fluid but not serum demonstrate intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, which is why paired samples are analysed in suspected multiple sclerosis.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. The Special Senses and States of Brain Activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which step in thyroid hormone synthesis is inhibited by carbimazole?
questions.concept: Because stored hormone is unaffected, the clinical effect is delayed by weeks, which is why beta-blockade is used for symptom control while waiting.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which is the most abundant and which the most active thyroid hormone in the circulation?
options: Thyroxine is most abundant while triiodothyronine is more active, most of it formed by peripheral deiodination
questions.concept: Illness, starvation and drugs such as propranolol and amiodarone shift deiodination toward the inactive reverse form, producing the low triiodothyronine of non-thyroidal illness.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormone raises serum calcium by increasing bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and calcitriol synthesis?
questions.concept: Parathyroid hormone also lowers phosphate by inhibiting proximal reabsorption, which distinguishes primary hyperparathyroidism from other causes of hypercalcaemia biochemically.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which enzyme in the kidney is stimulated by parathyroid hormone to activate vitamin D, and what inhibits it?
options: 1-alpha hydroxylase, inhibited by FGF23 and by calcitriol itself
questions.concept: Loss of renal 1-alpha hydroxylation is why chronic kidney disease causes hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and why active analogues rather than cholecalciferol are used.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which zone of the adrenal cortex produces aldosterone, and what is its principal regulator?
options: The zona glomerulosa, regulated by angiotensin II and potassium rather than by ACTH
The zona fasciculata, regulated by ACTH
The zona reticularis, regulated by potassium
The medulla, regulated by sympathetic outflow
questions.concept: Because ACTH is not the main driver, aldosterone secretion is largely preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency, which is why salt-wasting is a feature of primary but not secondary disease.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which phase of insulin secretion is lost earliest in type 2 diabetes?
options: The first phase, the rapid release of pre-formed insulin granules after a glucose load
questions.concept: Loss of the early spike allows an exaggerated postprandial glucose excursion, which is why postprandial hyperglycaemia often precedes fasting hyperglycaemia in the natural history.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which effect of cortisol explains its use in reducing cerebral oedema around a tumour?
options: Reduction of capillary permeability and of inflammatory mediator production
questions.concept: Cortisol is effective in vasogenic oedema surrounding tumours and abscesses but not in cytotoxic oedema after ischaemia, which is why steroids are not used in acute stroke or head injury.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does chronic hypocalcaemia in chronic kidney disease not simply respond to calcium supplementation?
options: Impaired calcitriol synthesis limits intestinal calcium absorption, and phosphate retention with high FGF23 must also be corrected
Calcium is not absorbed at all
questions.concept: Management therefore combines phosphate restriction and binders with active vitamin D analogues and sometimes calcimimetics, rather than calcium alone.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Why does the Wolff-Chaikoff effect limit the usefulness of iodide as a long-term antithyroid treatment?
options: The inhibition of organification is transient and escape occurs within 10 to 14 days
Iodide is toxic to the liver
questions.concept: The transient nature is precisely why Lugol's iodine is confined to short preoperative preparation and to thyroid storm, given after a thionamide has blocked synthesis.
questions.reference: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e, Ch. Thyroid, Adrenal and Pancreatic Hormones
